# The computing environment: HPC, remote development, and cloud {#sec-computing}

Genetic data is too large and too sensitive for a laptop, so your analyses run somewhere else: on a shared high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, in a big-data platform, or in a cloud workspace next to the data. Learn to submit and monitor batch jobs, keep your software environment reproducible, and edit code remotely. Then the location of the computer stops mattering.

## Why a cluster

You use a cluster for three reasons: the data does not fit on your machine, the work splits into many independent pieces, and the data is not allowed to leave a controlled environment. A GWAS on 500,000 people is 22 chromosomes, each split into chunks, each run as a separate job.

A cluster has three kinds of parts:

- **Login nodes**, where you connect by SSH, edit files, and submit jobs. They are shared by everyone, so never run heavy work there.
- **Compute nodes**, where jobs actually run. You reach them only through the scheduler.
- **A shared parallel file system** (GPFS, Lustre, or similar), mounted on every node, so a job sees the same files you do.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    U["Your laptop"] -->|"SSH or VPN"| L["Login node"]
    L -->|"bsub or sbatch"| S["Scheduler"]
    S --> C1["Compute node"]
    S --> C2["Compute node"]
    S --> C3["Compute node"]
    L --- FS[("Shared file system")]
    C1 --- FS
    C2 --- FS
    C3 --- FS
```

A **scheduler** decides which job runs where and when, based on what you request (cores, memory, time) and on fair-share policies. Many institutional clusters are federations: pools of nodes bought by different groups, each reached through its own **queue**. Which queues you may use depends on your group membership.

## Submitting jobs with LSF

IBM Spectrum LSF is common in academic medical centers; SLURM is the most common elsewhere. The ideas are identical. A job is a shell script plus a resource request.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#BSUB -J gwas_chr22                # job name
#BSUB -q normal                    # queue
#BSUB -n 4                         # cores
#BSUB -R "rusage[mem=16000]"       # memory, in MB on most sites
#BSUB -R "span[hosts=1]"           # all cores on one node
#BSUB -W 8:00                      # wall time, hours:minutes
#BSUB -o logs/%J.out               # stdout, %J = job ID
#BSUB -e logs/%J.err               # stderr
set -euo pipefail

module load plink/2.0
plink2 --pfile data/chr22 --glm --threads 4 --memory 14000 --out results/chr22
```

Submit it with `bsub < job.sh` (the `<` lets LSF read the `#BSUB` lines). Then monitor:

```bash
bjobs                       # your pending and running jobs
bjobs -l 123456             # full detail: host, limits, reason pending
bjobs -o "id stat queue exec_host"
bpeek 123456                # stdout of a running job
bhist -l 123456             # history after it finishes
bkill 123456                # cancel
bqueues                     # queues you can see and their limits
bhosts                      # nodes and their load
bsub -q interactive -Is bash    # an interactive shell on a compute node
```

Memory units in `rusage[mem=...]` depend on how the site configured LSF (MB is most common). Check your cluster's documentation and test with a small job first.

**Array jobs** run the same script many times with a different index. They are the natural shape for per-chromosome work.

```bash
#BSUB -J "gwas[1-22]"
#BSUB -o logs/%J_%I.out
CHR=${LSB_JOBINDEX}
plink2 --pfile data/chr${CHR} --glm --out results/chr${CHR}
```

Use `"gwas[1-22]%5"` to run at most five at a time, and `bkill "123456[7]"` to cancel one element.

## SLURM equivalents

If you move between clusters, this table covers most daily use.

| Task | LSF | SLURM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Submit a script | `bsub < job.sh` | `sbatch job.sh` |
| Directive prefix | `#BSUB` | `#SBATCH` |
| Queue / partition | `-q normal` | `-p normal` |
| Cores | `-n 4` | `-c 4` (`--cpus-per-task`) |
| Memory | `-R "rusage[mem=16000]"` | `--mem=16G` |
| Wall time | `-W 8:00` | `-t 08:00:00` |
| Job name | `-J name` | `-J name` |
| Output log | `-o logs/%J.out` | `-o logs/%j.out` |
| Array job | `-J "name[1-22]"`, `$LSB_JOBINDEX` | `--array=1-22`, `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` |
| List my jobs | `bjobs` | `squeue -u $USER` |
| Job detail | `bjobs -l ID` | `scontrol show job ID` |
| Finished job accounting | `bhist -l ID`, `bacct` | `sacct -j ID` |
| Cancel | `bkill ID` | `scancel ID` |
| Queues / partitions | `bqueues` | `sinfo` |
| Interactive shell | `bsub -Is bash` | `srun --pty bash` |

::: {.callout-tip title="In practice"}
Size requests from a real run. Submit one chromosome, then read the peak memory and run time from `bjobs -l` or `sacct`. Request about 20–30% more than the peak. Over-asking makes you wait longer in the queue; under-asking gets the job killed near the end.
:::

## Software: modules, conda, and containers

Use the lightest tool that pins your versions.

- **Environment modules** (`module avail`, `module load R/4.3`, `module list`) give you centrally installed software. Load them inside the job script, not only in your login shell.
- **Conda** or **mamba** environments install your own Python and R stacks without admin rights. Export them with `conda env export > environment.yml`, and point your package directories at project storage because home quotas are small.
- **Containers** freeze the whole operating system layer. On HPC you run them with **Apptainer** (formerly Singularity), which runs as your user and can pull Docker images.

```bash
# TAG: pick an exact version tag from quay.io/biocontainers/bcftools
apptainer pull bcftools.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/bcftools:TAG
apptainer exec --bind $PWD bcftools.sif bcftools --version
```

Write a small `start.sh` in each project that loads modules and activates the environment, and `source` it at the top of every job script. One file then defines the environment for both you and your jobs.

## Storage tiers

Clusters have several file systems with different rules. Names vary; the roles do not.

| Tier | Typical size | Backed up | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Home | Small, tens of GB | Usually | Configuration, scripts, small environments |
| Project or group | Large, tens to hundreds of TB | Often, or snapshots | Shared datasets, code, final results |
| Scratch | Large, fast | No, purged on a schedule | Intermediate files you can regenerate |
| Node-local scratch | Per node, fastest | No, deleted after the job | Heavy temporary I/O inside one job |

Keep raw data read-only in a dedicated directory and never run analyses inside it. Write intermediates to scratch, then copy what you need to project space. Move files with `rsync -avP` or `scp`, and only data your access agreements allow off the cluster.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
Long interactive work on a login node, or a `for` loop that runs 22 chromosomes there, gets your processes killed and slows everyone else. Use an interactive job or a batch job. To survive a dropped connection, start `tmux` or `screen` first.
:::

## VS Code Remote-SSH

The Remote-SSH extension runs VS Code's editor on your laptop and its server, terminal, and language tools on the cluster. You edit remote files as if they were local.

First, create a key pair on your laptop and copy the public key to the cluster, if your site allows key authentication:

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop"
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub username@hpc-login.example.edu
```

Then describe the host in `~/.ssh/config`:

```text
Host hpc
    HostName hpc-login.example.edu
    User username
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p
    ControlPersist 4h
```

Now `ssh hpc` works in a terminal. In VS Code, install "Remote - SSH", run **Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...**, and pick `hpc`. Many institutions require a VPN first; some require two-factor authentication on every login, which `ControlMaster` reduces to once per session.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as VS Code on laptop
    participant L as Login node
    participant C as Compute node
    V->>L: SSH using ~/.ssh/config
    L-->>V: VS Code server starts in home
    V->>L: Edit files, open terminal
    L->>C: bsub or sbatch from the terminal
    C-->>L: Results on shared file system
```

Install the Python, R, and Jupyter extensions on the remote side, select the interpreter from your conda environment, and keep `~/.vscode-server` from filling your home quota. For a Jupyter server on a compute node, start it with `jupyter lab --no-browser --port=8888` inside an interactive job, then forward the port: `ssh -N -L 8888:<node>:8888 hpc`.

## Databricks and Spark for big tables

Electronic health record (EHR) extracts are billions of rows: every diagnosis, lab, and medication for every patient. A data platform such as **Databricks** runs **Apache Spark** over tables stored in cloud object storage, so a query is split across many machines.

You work in notebooks (SQL, Python, R) attached to a compute cluster. Tables live in a **catalog**, organized as `catalog.schema.table`, with permissions set per schema. The common pattern is to filter and aggregate in Spark, then hand a small result to pandas or R.

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
dx = spark.table("research.ehr.diagnoses")
cases = (dx.filter(F.col("icd10_code").startswith("E11"))
           .groupBy("person_id")
           .agg(F.countDistinct("encounter_date").alias("n_dates"))
           .filter("n_dates >= 2"))
cases.toPandas().to_csv("t2d_cases.csv", index=False)  # only after aggregating
```

Avoid `.toPandas()` or `collect()` on large tables: it pulls everything into one machine's memory. Genotype-scale work fits better on the HPC cluster or on Hail.

## Workflows and the cloud

When a pipeline has many steps and must run the same way on hundreds of samples, write it in a workflow language. **WDL** (Workflow Description Language, <https://openwdl.org/>) describes **tasks** (a command with inputs, outputs, and a container) and a **workflow** that wires them together. **Cromwell** and **miniwdl** execute it locally, on HPC, or in the cloud. Nextflow and Snakemake fill the same role with different syntax.

```text
version 1.0
task count_variants {
  input { File vcf  String image }
  command <<< bcftools view -H ~{vcf} | wc -l >>>
  output { Int n = read_int(stdout()) }
  runtime {
    docker: image
    memory: "2 GB"
  }
}
workflow count {
  input { Array[File] vcfs  String image }
  scatter (v in vcfs) { call count_variants { input: vcf = v, image = image } }
  output { Array[Int] counts = count_variants.n }
}
```

The large genomic resources now keep data in the cloud and bring you to it, a model called a **trusted research environment** (@sec-biobanks).

- **Terra**, developed by the Broad Institute with partners, runs WDL on Google Cloud, with notebooks. NHGRI's **AnVIL** and the All of Us Researcher Workbench are built on it.
- **DNAnexus** runs the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform, with apps, Spark, and Jupyter.

In the cloud, files are objects addressed by full URLs (`gs://bucket/path/file.vcf.gz`, `s3://...`), not directories. A list of input files for a workflow must contain full paths. You pay for compute and storage by the hour, so stop idle notebooks and delete intermediates.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    D[("Controlled data<br/>in cloud storage")] --> W["Workspace<br/>notebooks + workflows"]
    W --> R["Aggregate results"]
    R -->|"review rules"| E["Export"]
    W -.-x X["Individual-level data<br/>cannot leave"]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Try it"}
Write an LSF array job (or SLURM, if that is what you have) that downloads the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 VCF for chromosomes 20, 21, and 22 and runs `bcftools stats` on each. Size it from a single test run, then rewrite the same logic as a WDL `scatter` and run it locally with `miniwdl run`.
:::
